shortDescription: Banks are seeking clarity on whether hedges against interest payments on FCNR(B) deposits will attract the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) expanded Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), as lenders begin setting aside cash under the new rules and assess the cost of hedging foreign-currency liabilities…

children: Banks are seeking clarity on whether hedges against interest payments on FCNR(B) deposits will attract the Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) expanded Foreign Exchange Risk Reserve (FERR), as lenders begin setting aside cash under the new rules and assess the cost of hedging foreign-currency liabilities., said bankers.

The uncertainty follows the RBI’s October 12 directions extending FERR to eligible rupee-linked foreign exchange derivative contracts that authorised dealers undertake to hedge currency risks on their own assets and liabilities. Banks want to know whether this also covers hedges against interest payments on FCNR(B) deposits.

The October 12 directions followed measures announced on October 10 to curb speculative activity and moderate pressure on the rupee. The RBI barred the rebooking of cancelled rupee-linked derivative contracts, while allowing rollovers at maturity, and reduced the threshold for taking foreign exchange derivative positions without establishing underlying exposure from $100 million to $5 million across authorised dealers and exchange-traded rupee derivatives. It also introduced FERR for eligible client derivative contracts exceeding $2 million where users buy foreign currency against the rupee to hedge current account transactions.
FCNR(B) hedges: Higher costs, liquidity concerns

Under the RBI’s FCNR(B) swap facility, banks raise dollar deposits from non-resident Indians and convert the funds into rupees through swaps, allowing them to deploy the proceeds in domestic assets. They earn returns in rupees but must pay interest to depositors in dollars, exposing them to the risk that a weaker rupee will increase the cost of those payments.

Banks therefore hedge their dollar interest obligations. The uncertainty is whether these hedges fall within the expanded FERR requirement for derivatives that banks use to manage currency risks on their own assets and liabilities.

A second complication is how the underlying transaction is classified. While the deposit principal may be treated as a capital account transaction, the interest or coupon payment may be treated as a current account transaction. Banks want the RBI to clarify whether this distinction affects the applicability of FERR to hedges on interest payments.

“Banks need to hedge these foreign-currency interest payments but are unsure whether such transactions will attract FERR under the expanded directions covering their own assets and liabilities,” a treasury head at a private bank said. “If that is the case, we need to put FERR for this hedging interest also.”
Higher hedging costs, less cash for treasury operations

The FERR requirement means banks must set aside cash equivalent to 20 percent of the rupee value of each eligible derivative contract and maintain it with the RBI until the contract terminates. This ties up funds that could otherwise be deployed in lending or other treasury activities.

For banks with large derivative books and substantial customer hedging flows, the requirement could raise the cost of managing currency risk. Lenders may pass on some of the additional cost through wider bid-offer spreads and more expensive forward hedging, making it costlier for businesses to hedge foreign-currency payments and receipts.
“The concern is that hedging could become uneconomical if banks must lock up additional cash against contracts until maturity,” a treasury head at another private bank said.

Banks are also seeking clarity on how to calculate and recover the cost of maintaining FERR. They want to know whether the cost should be linked to a benchmark such as the marginal standing facility (MSF) rate, marginal cost of funds-based lending rate (MCLR) or external benchmark-linked lending rate (EBLR), or to a rate specified by the RBI.

The impact will depend on which contracts are considered eligible and how the reserve is calculated. Until the scope is clear, banks face uncertainty over how much additional cash they may need to set aside for hedging their own foreign-currency liabilities and how much of the resulting cost can be passed on to customers.

title: Banks seek clarity on FCNR(B) interest hedges under RBI’s expanded forex rules
